topic: Commercial certificate: eligibility, experience and medical

notes.front: What is a commercial pilot certificate?
notes.back: The pilot certificate whose holder may act as pilot in command carrying persons or property for compensation or hire.
notes.explanation: Part 61 attaches a condition: the holder must also be qualified under the other parts of the regulations that apply to the operation.
notes.example: Like a private pilot certificate, but with the bar on being paid to fly lifted: the step taken before flying as a job.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: A person who holds a commercial pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft— (i) Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a technically advanced airplane (TAA)?
notes.back: An airplane equipped with an electronically advanced avionics system.
notes.explanation: Part 61 defines it by its avionics alone; §61.129(j) then lists the installed components that system must include.
notes.example: Like a trainer with a glass cockpit and an autopilot, rather than one with a panel of round-dial gauges.
notes.evidence: Technically advanced airplane (TAA) means an airplane equipped with an electronically advanced avionics system.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the minimum age to take the Commercial Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.explanation: The Testing Matrix lists an age for each test; for this one it is lower than the age for the certificate itself.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (revised 9/25/26), "Commercial Pilot & Military Competence"
notes.evidence: CAX Commercial Pilot Airplane 100 16 2.5 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many questions does the Commercial Pilot Airplane knowledge test have?
notes.explanation: The Testing Matrix gives the number of questions beside the test code, the age, the allotted time and the passing grade.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (revised 9/25/26), "Commercial Pilot & Military Competence"
notes.evidence: CAX Commercial Pilot Airplane 100 16 2.5 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much time is allotted for the Commercial Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: 2.5 hours.
notes.explanation: The allotted time is taken from the Testing Matrix, which the Federal Aviation Administration names as holding the correct figure.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (revised 9/25/26), "Commercial Pilot & Military Competence"
notes.evidence: CAX Commercial Pilot Airplane 100 16 2.5 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the passing grade for the Commercial Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.explanation: The Testing Matrix lists the passing grade in the last column of each test's row.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (revised 9/25/26), "Commercial Pilot & Military Competence"
notes.evidence: CAX Commercial Pilot Airplane 100 16 2.5 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two acceptable forms of authorization for a first attempt at the Commercial Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: A ground-school graduation certificate or statement of accomplishment; an instructor's written statement or logbook endorsement.
notes.explanation: Either document shows the ground training or home study is done and, for the instructor's statement, that the applicant is prepared.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (revised 9/25/26), "Commercial Pilot & Military Competence"
notes.evidence: Written statement or logbook endorsement from an authorized ground or flight instructor certifying that the applicant completed an applicable ground training or home study course and is prepared for the knowledge test.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How old must a person be to be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate?
notes.back: At least 18.
notes.explanation: Age heads the list of eligibility requirements in §61.123, which goes on to language, endorsements, tests and experience.
notes.evidence: To be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate, a person must: (a) Be at least 18 years of age;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What English-language ability must a commercial pilot applicant have?
notes.back: Be able to read, speak, write and understand English.
notes.explanation: All four abilities are listed; a medical reason for missing one is handled by operating limitations rather than refusal.
notes.evidence: Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language. If the applicant is unable to meet one of these requirements due to medical reasons, then the Administrator may place such operating limitations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If a commercial applicant cannot meet one English requirement for medical reasons, what may the Administrator do?
notes.back: Place on the certificate the operating limitations necessary for safe operation of the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The rule allows the certificate with limits instead of barring the applicant outright.
notes.evidence: the Administrator may place such operating limitations on that applicant's pilot certificate as are necessary for the safe operation of the aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What pilot certificate must a commercial applicant already hold?
notes.back: At least a private pilot certificate issued under part 61 (or meet the requirements of §61.73).
notes.explanation: The commercial certificate builds on the private one: §61.123 makes holding it an eligibility requirement.
notes.evidence: Hold at least a private pilot certificate issued under this part or meet the requirements of § 61.73
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Before the commercial knowledge test, what must the authorized instructor's logbook endorsement certify?
notes.back: That the person is prepared for the required knowledge test for the category and class rating sought.
notes.explanation: The same instructor must also have given the ground training or reviewed the home study on the §61.125 knowledge areas.
notes.evidence: (c) Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the required ground training or reviewed the person's home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in § 61.125 of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought; and (2) Certified that the person is prepared for the required knowledge test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must the instructor who endorses a commercial applicant for the practical test have done?
notes.back: Conducted the training on the §61.127(b) areas of operation and certified the person is prepared for the practical test.
notes.explanation: The practical-test endorsement mirrors the knowledge-test one, but rests on flight training on areas of operation instead of knowledge areas.
notes.evidence: (e) Receive the required training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the training on the areas of operation listed in § 61.127(b) of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought; and (2) Certified that the person is prepared for the required practical test.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: By when must a commercial applicant meet the aeronautical experience requirements?
notes.back: Before applying for the practical test.
notes.explanation: The experience of §61.129 is a gate to the practical test, not something that may be completed afterwards.
notes.evidence: Meet the aeronautical experience requirements of this subpart that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought before applying for the practical test;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On what does the commercial knowledge test examine the applicant?
notes.back: The aeronautical knowledge areas listed in §61.125.
notes.explanation: Eligibility requires passing the test on that list, so §61.125 is in effect the test's syllabus.
notes.evidence: Pass the required knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in § 61.125 of this part;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: From whom must a commercial applicant receive and log ground training, and what may replace it?
notes.back: An authorized instructor; or the applicant may complete a home-study course.
notes.explanation: Either route covers the §61.125(b) knowledge areas for the category and class rating sought.
notes.evidence: must receive and log ground training from an authorized instructor, or complete a home-study course, on the aeronautical knowledge areas of paragraph (b) of this section
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which regulations are a commercial aeronautical knowledge area?
notes.back: The Federal Aviation Regulations relating to commercial pilot privileges, limitations and flight operations.
notes.explanation: It is the first item on the §61.125(b) list, and it is the subject of the next topic of this deck.
notes.evidence: Applicable Federal Aviation Regulations of this chapter that relate to commercial pilot privileges, limitations, and flight operations;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Whose accident reporting requirements are a commercial knowledge area?
notes.back: Those of the National Transportation Safety Board.
notes.explanation: §61.125(b)(2) names the board's requirements, not those of the regulator that issues the certificate.
notes.evidence: Accident reporting requirements of the National Transportation Safety Board;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the meteorology knowledge area for the commercial certificate include?
notes.back: Recognising critical weather situations, windshear recognition and avoidance, and using weather reports and forecasts.
notes.explanation: The list names windshear on its own, beside the general use of reports and forecasts.
notes.evidence: Meteorology to include recognition of critical weather situations, windshear recognition and avoidance, and the use of aeronautical weather reports and forecasts;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides the use of performance charts, §61.125(b) lists the significance and effects of {{c1::exceeding aircraft performance limitations}}.
notes.explanation: The commercial list goes beyond reading charts to what happens when the limits they show are exceeded.
notes.evidence: Significance and effects of exceeding aircraft performance limitations;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: {{c1::Night and high-altitude}} operations are a commercial aeronautical knowledge area.
notes.explanation: The item sits in §61.125(b) between manoeuvres and emergency operations and National Airspace System procedures.
notes.evidence: Night and high-altitude operations;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which §61.125(b) knowledge area applies only to lighter-than-air ratings?
notes.back: Procedures for flight and ground training for lighter-than-air ratings.
notes.explanation: It is the last item on the list; an airplane applicant is examined on the areas that apply to the rating sought.
notes.evidence: Procedures for flight and ground training for lighter-than-air ratings.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much flight time must an applicant for a commercial certificate with an airplane single-engine rating log?
notes.back: At least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot.
notes.explanation: The 250 hours is a total; §61.129(a) then sets minimums inside it for powered, pilot-in-command and cross-country time.
notes.evidence: must log at least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot that consists of at least:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many of the 250 hours must be in powered aircraft, and how many of those in airplanes?
notes.back: 100 hours in powered aircraft, of which 50 hours must be in airplanes.
notes.explanation: Hours in aircraft that are not powered do not count toward this 100, and half of the 100 must be in airplanes.
notes.evidence: 100 hours in powered aircraft, of which 50 hours must be in airplanes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much pilot-in-command time does §61.129(a) require, and how much of it in airplanes?
notes.back: 100 hours, including at least 50 hours in airplanes.
notes.explanation: The cross-country requirement sits inside these same 100 pilot-in-command hours.
notes.evidence: 100 hours of pilot-in-command flight time, which includes at least— (i) 50 hours in airplanes; and
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much cross-country pilot-in-command time is required, and how much of it in airplanes?
notes.back: 50 hours cross-country, of which at least 10 hours in airplanes.
notes.explanation: Only 10 of the 50 cross-country hours need be in airplanes, a smaller share than the 50 of 100 for pilot-in-command time overall.
notes.evidence: 50 hours in cross-country flight of which at least 10 hours must be in airplanes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many hours of training on the §61.127(b)(1) areas of operation must a single-engine commercial applicant log?
notes.back: At least 20 hours.
notes.explanation: The 20 hours contain the instrument, complex-or-TAA, dual cross-country and checkride-preparation training.
notes.evidence: 20 hours of training on the areas of operation listed in § 61.127(b)(1) of this part that includes at least—
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much instrument training must a commercial applicant receive, and how much of it in a single-engine airplane?
notes.back: 10 hours, of which 5 hours must be in a single-engine airplane.
notes.explanation: The rule fixes only where 5 of the 10 hours are flown; all 10 hours use a view-limiting device.
notes.evidence: Five hours of the 10 hours required on instrument training must be in a single engine airplane;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The 10 hours of commercial instrument training are flown using a {{c1::view-limiting device}}.
notes.explanation: The same sentence lists what the training covers, starting with attitude instrument flying and partial panel skills.
notes.evidence: Ten hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device including attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides attitude instrument flying and partial panel skills, what two things must the commercial instrument training include?
notes.back: Recovery from unusual flight attitudes, and intercepting and tracking navigational systems.
notes.explanation: These four items together make up the content §61.129(a)(3)(i) prescribes for the 10 hours.
notes.evidence: including attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills, recovery from unusual flight attitudes, and intercepting and tracking navigational systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In which airplanes may the 10 hours of §61.129(a)(3)(ii) training be flown?
notes.back: A complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane or a TAA meeting §61.129(j), or any combination.
notes.explanation: The rule does not demand a complex airplane: a TAA or a turbine airplane is an equal choice, and the three may be mixed.
notes.evidence: 10 hours of training in a complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane, or a technically advanced airplane (TAA) that meets the requirements of paragraph (j) of this section, or any combination thereof.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must be true of the airplane used for the 10 hours of complex, turbine or TAA training?
notes.back: It must be appropriate to land or sea for the rating sought.
notes.explanation: A land rating calls for training in a landplane and a sea rating in a seaplane.
notes.evidence: The airplane must be appropriate to land or sea for the rating sought;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What daytime cross-country training flight does §61.129(a)(3) require?
notes.back: One 2-hour flight in a single-engine airplane, more than 100 nautical miles straight-line from the original departure point.
notes.explanation: Both limits apply: the duration and a straight-line distance from the departure point, not the distance flown.
notes.evidence: One 2-hour cross country flight in a single engine airplane in daytime conditions that consists of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What nighttime cross-country training flight does §61.129(a)(3) require?
notes.back: One 2-hour flight in a single-engine airplane at night, more than 100 nautical miles straight-line from the original departure point.
notes.explanation: It repeats the day flight's duration and distance in nighttime conditions.
notes.evidence: One 2-hour cross country flight in a single engine airplane in nighttime conditions that consists of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much instruction in preparation for the commercial practical test is required, and when?
notes.back: Three hours in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor, within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test.
notes.explanation: The window is counted in calendar months back from the test month, so the preparation must be recent.
notes.evidence: Three hours in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor in preparation for the practical test within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which 10 hours does §61.129(a)(4) require of a single-engine commercial applicant?
notes.back: 10 hours of solo flight, or 10 hours performing the duties of pilot in command with an authorized instructor on board.
notes.explanation: Either kind of time counts, and both are flown in a single-engine airplane.
notes.evidence: Ten hours of solo flight time in a single engine airplane or 10 hours of flight time performing the duties of pilot in command in a single engine airplane with an authorized instructor on board
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May the 10 hours of solo or pilot-in-command-duty time also count toward the 100 hours of pilot-in-command time?
notes.back: Yes; either kind may be credited toward the §61.129(a)(2) requirement.
notes.explanation: The regulation says so in a parenthesis, so the same hours serve both requirements.
notes.evidence: (either of which may be credited towards the flight time requirement under paragraph (a)(2) of this section)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What total distance must the commercial solo (or pilot-in-command) cross-country cover?
notes.back: Not less than 300 nautical miles.
notes.explanation: The total is only one of three conditions; the number of landings and the straight-line leg also count.
notes.evidence: One cross-country flight of not less than 300 nautical miles total distance, with landings at a minimum of three points
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At how many points must the commercial long cross-country land?
notes.back: At a minimum of three points.
notes.explanation: Three landing points make a flight with several legs, one of which must reach far from the start.
notes.evidence: with landings at a minimum of three points, one of which is a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How far from the original departure point must one landing point of the commercial long cross-country be?
notes.back: At least 250 nautical miles in a straight line.
notes.explanation: The distance is measured in a straight line from where the flight began, not along the route flown.
notes.evidence: one of which is a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If the commercial long cross-country is flown in Hawaii, what straight-line distance must the longest segment have?
notes.back: At least 150 nautical miles.
notes.explanation: The regulation makes this single exception to the 250-mile figure for flights in Hawaii.
notes.evidence: However, if this requirement is being met in Hawaii, the longest segment need only have a straight-line distance of at least 150 nautical miles;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much night flying must the commercial solo (or pilot-in-command) time include?
notes.back: 5 hours in night VFR conditions.
notes.explanation: The night hours come with a set number of takeoffs and landings at a towered airport.
notes.evidence: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many night takeoffs and landings must the commercial applicant make, and where?
notes.back: 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at an airport with an operating control tower.
notes.explanation: Each landing must also involve a flight in the traffic pattern.
notes.evidence: with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which TAA component must include, at a minimum, an airspeed indicator, attitude indicator and altimeter, among other instruments?
notes.back: An electronic primary flight display (PFD).
notes.explanation: The display brings the basic flight instruments onto one electronic screen.
notes.evidence: An electronic Primary Flight Display (PFD) that includes, at a minimum, an airspeed indicator, turn coordinator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A TAA's primary flight display includes at least an airspeed indicator, turn coordinator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter and {{c1::vertical speed indicator}}.
notes.explanation: These are the six basic flight instruments, all required on the electronic display.
notes.evidence: an airspeed indicator, turn coordinator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a TAA's electronic multifunction display show at a minimum?
notes.back: A moving map using Global Positioning System navigation, with the aircraft position displayed.
notes.explanation: The multifunction display is the second screen of the system, beside the primary flight display.
notes.evidence: An electronic Multifunction Display (MFD) that includes, at a minimum, a moving map using Global Positioning System (GPS) navigation with the aircraft position displayed;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What autopilot must a TAA have?
notes.back: A two-axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system.
notes.explanation: An autopilot that is not integrated with the navigation and heading guidance does not meet the rule.
notes.evidence: A two axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system; and
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does §61.129(j) require of a TAA's primary flight display and multifunction display elements?
notes.back: They must be continuously visible.
notes.explanation: Both elements must be in view at all times, not only when selected.
notes.evidence: The display elements described in paragraphs (j)(1) and (2) of this section must be continuously visible.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Outside a part 142 training centre course, how much simulator or flight training device time may count toward the commercial airplane total?
notes.back: A maximum of 50 hours, from an authorized instructor in a device representing that class of airplane.
notes.explanation: The device must represent the class of airplane for the rating sought.
notes.evidence: Credit a maximum of 50 hours toward the total aeronautical experience requirements for an airplane or powered-lift rating, provided the aeronautical experience was obtained from an authorized instructor in a full flight simulator or flight training device
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In a part 142 training centre course, how much simulator or flight training device time may count toward the commercial airplane total?
notes.back: A maximum of 100 hours.
notes.explanation: The part 142 figure is twice the 50 hours allowed outside such a course.
notes.evidence: Credit a maximum of 100 hours toward the total aeronautical experience requirements of this section for an airplane and powered-lift rating
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After how many hours is a graduate of an approved part 142 commercial course considered to meet the total experience requirement?
notes.back: 190 hours (unless fewer are approved).
notes.explanation: The reduced total applies only to a completed approved part 142 course for the certificate and rating sought.
notes.evidence: an applicant for the commercial pilot certificate with the airplane or powered-lift rating who has completed 190 hours of aeronautical experience is considered to have met the total aeronautical experience requirements of this section
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Who is not required to meet the commercial night flight training requirements, subject to limitations?
notes.back: A person who receives flight training in and resides in the State of Alaska.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must hold: training in Alaska and residence there.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.131 Exceptions to the night flying requirements (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: a person is not required to comply with the night flight training requirements of this subpart if the person receives flight training in and resides in the State of Alaska.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What limitation may be placed on the certificate of an Alaska pilot who has not met the night training requirements?
notes.back: "Night flying prohibited."
notes.explanation: The certificate is issued, but without night privileges until the training is done.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.131 Exceptions to the night flying requirements (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: May be issued a pilot certificate with the limitation “night flying prohibited.”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within what period must an Alaska pilot issued a certificate without night training complete it?
notes.back: Within the 12-calendar-month period after the certificate is issued.
notes.explanation: At the end of that period the certificate becomes invalid for use until the night training is completed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.131 Exceptions to the night flying requirements (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: Must comply with the appropriate night flight training requirements of this subpart within the 12-calendar-month period after the issuance of the pilot certificate. At the end of that period, the certificate will become invalid for use
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How may an Alaska pilot have the "night flying prohibited" limitation removed?
notes.back: Complete the night training and present to an examiner an instructor's endorsement verifying it.
notes.explanation: Training alone is not enough: an examiner must see the logbook or training record endorsement.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.131 Exceptions to the night flying requirements (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: Accomplishes the appropriate night flight training requirements of this subpart; and (ii) Presents to an examiner a logbook or training record endorsement from an authorized instructor
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What class of medical certificate must a pilot hold, at least, to exercise commercial pilot privileges in an airplane?
notes.back: A second-class medical certificate.
notes.explanation: The requirement covers commercial privileges in any aircraft other than a balloon or glider.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Must hold at least a second class medical certificate when exercising: (i) Second-in-command privileges of an airline transport pilot certificate in part 121 of this chapter (other than operations specified in paragraph (a)(1)(ii) of this section); (ii) Privileges of a commercial pilot certificate in an aircraft other than a balloon or glider
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When does a second-class medical certificate expire for commercial pilot privileges?
notes.back: At the end of the last day of the 12th month after the month of the examination, at any age.
notes.explanation: The row applies at any age; the same certificate then serves private privileges for longer.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)(2)
notes.evidence: (i) Any age an airline transport pilot certificate for second-in-command privileges (other than the operations specified in paragraph (d)(1) of this section), a commercial pilot certificate (other than a commercial pilot certificate with a balloon rating when conducting flight training), a flight engineer certificate, or an air traffic control tower operator certificate 12th month after the month
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.back: The Testing Matrix figure: the Federal Aviation Administration lists the standards' allotted time for this test as incorrect.
notes.explanation: The correction table points to itself and to the Matrix for the correct allotted times.
notes.source: FAA, ACS Knowledge Test Table: Correct Allotted Times (updated October 2024)
notes.evidence: Allotted times are incorrect, in the corresponding ACS, for the knowledge tests listed below. Correct allotted times are shown in this table and in the FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix.

notes.front: For one second-class medical held by a pilot under 40, how do the commercial and private expiry dates compare?
notes.back: Commercial privileges: end of the 12th month after the exam month. Private privileges: end of the 60th month.
notes.explanation: The §61.23(d) table sets a period for each kind of operation, not one date for the certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)
